evals.prompt:
We're Harborlane, shipment-tracking SaaS. Our /v2 API has been live with 6 design-partner customers for about 9 months and we open it to anyone in 5 weeks. Roughly what it looks like:

- GET /shipments returns created_at, updated_at, carrier_id
- GET /carriers returns createdAt, updatedAt, shipmentCount
- POST /shipments/{id}/cancel-shipment, and also POST /carriers/{id}/verify-carrier
- DELETE /webhooks/{id} returns 200 with {"ok": false, "message": "webhook attached to active subscription"} when it can't delete
- GET /shipments/{id}/events/{eventId}/attachments/{attachmentId}/thumbnails

We already know clients parse createdAt off /carriers because two of them emailed us about its timezone format. We've never adopted a style guide of any kind. Go through this and tell us what we have to fix before we open it up.
evals.expected_output: A scoped review report: public x beta-to-GA posture stated as blocking, findings bucketed Must-change vs Improvement with a cited rule each, the casing split flagged as a consistency Must-change without picking a winning casing, and its fix routed through deprecation machinery because clients already observe the field.
expectations: Sorts findings into exactly two buckets, named Must-change and Improvement
Assigns no numeric score, letter grade, percentage, or Critical/High/Medium/Low severity scale to the surface or to any finding
States that the surface being publicly consumable and about to open makes this a blocking review rather than advisory feedback
Flags the created_at versus createdAt split across /shipments and /carriers as a Must-change
Declines to declare either snake_case or camelCase the correct convention, citing consistency of the choice as the rule instead
States that renaming createdAt is itself a breaking change because clients already observe that field
Routes the casing fix through deprecation or versioning machinery rather than prescribing a silent in-place rename
Names samber/developer-platform-skills@api-versioning-policy as the owner of scheduling that removal
Flags DELETE /webhooks/{id} returning 200 with an error body and prescribes 409 with the standard error envelope instead
Flags cancel-shipment and verify-carrier as verbs in the URI and proposes one custom-method convention applied across every action endpoint
Flags the /shipments/{id}/events/{eventId}/attachments/{attachmentId}/thumbnails path as exceeding a 2-3 level nesting limit
States that because the team has adopted no rule corpus, findings cite this skill's own checklist items by name
Attaches a cited rule or precedent to every finding placed in the Must-change bucket
Presents findings in a table carrying finding, dimension, bucket, cited rule, and proposed fix

evals.prompt: I'm the new head of platform at Verrill Systems. Two years ago we had 3 backend teams; we now have 31 and about 19 of them ship something external-facing. Every team invented its own pagination and its own error body. I want to stand up a proper API design review board: a monthly meeting where teams bring designs, staffed by 5 senior architects, growing to 10 as load increases. I have real budget and roughly two quarters to get it running. What should the process look like?
evals.expected_output: A program design that replaces the monthly calendar cadence with audience x lifecycle triggers, refuses the committee-growth plan, promotes the certified federated reviewer pool for this scale while naming the answers that promoted it, and states the ladder ordering per axis out loud.
expectations: Rejects the proposed monthly meeting cadence and triggers review on audience and lifecycle stage instead of a calendar
States review is required at beta and at GA-if-changed, recommended at alpha, and skipped for internal-only surfaces
Rejects growing the architect group from 5 to 10 and states that growing a central committee is the one scaling move no studied company chose
Recommends the certified federated reviewer pool rung for this organization
Names the two-quarter runway, the budget, and the 31-team scale as the answers that promoted that rung above the default
States the maturity-ladder ordering explicitly in the text rather than leaving it implied by the order of a list
Gives separate orderings for efficiency and for effort or value, noting the federated pool loses every efficiency round while winning on value
Requires a shared, versioned rule corpus to exist before the reviewer pool grows
States that growing reviewers without a versioned corpus degrades turnaround time and guidance consistency together
Attributes the centralized-friction-point concession to Kenneth Auchenberg personally rather than to Stripe as a company
Requires publishing the escalation path and a named override authority up front
Places a spec linter first for mechanical checks and keeps semantic judgment with human reviewers
Gives turnaround guidance of under a week for small APIs, with a median past roughly 2 weeks signalling the program is too heavy
Recommends forking an existing public rule corpus rather than authoring one from a blank page

evals.prompt: Tessellate Health, 11 engineers across 2 backend teams, one public API for patient scheduling, about 40 endpoints. Our CTO read about Google's API readability certification and wants us to build the same thing: a written style guide, a certification process for reviewers, and embedded API champions per domain. I have maybe 3 days of my own time before the next sprint starts. Rank the options and tell me what to actually do.
evals.expected_output: A recommendation that steps down to a linter-only CI gate, removes the federated/certified rung from the menu outright rather than ranking it last, and supplies the concrete re-promotion trigger that would bring it back.
expectations: Removes the certified federated reviewer pool from the option menu entirely rather than ranking it last or parking it as a later phase
Justifies removal over demotion by noting a parked rung reappears as roadmap work that consumes corpus-writing time nobody needs yet
Gives an explicit re-promotion trigger: a third team shipping its own API surface, or median review turnaround past roughly 2 weeks
Recommends a linter-only CI gate rather than the default linter-plus-two-named-reviewers rung
Names the two-team scope and the 3-day effort ceiling as the answers that moved the recommendation down from the default rung
States that the semantic conversation still happens inside ordinary code review at this scale
Recommends forking a published corpus such as Zalando, Adidas, or Microsoft rather than writing a style guide from scratch
States the corpus must be adapted to the team's own articulated intent before it is enforced
States the ranking of the options explicitly rather than implying it through the order of a list
Declines to propose reviewer certification or per-domain embedded champions for an 11-engineer, two-team organization
Keeps the Must-change versus Improvement two-bucket model rather than introducing a numeric severity score
Characterizes the corpus-plus-linter setup as roughly an afternoon of work rather than a multi-week program

evals.prompt: Quick one. At Northmark we have an internal service API, /billing-internal, consumed only by our own web app and one nightly batch job. Both live in our monorepo, both deployed by us. It's at alpha and we intend to keep it internal permanently. Our new architecture lead wants it to clear the same blocking design review as our public partner API before it can deploy. The team says that's overkill and we're deadlocked. Settle it: what review, if any, does this need?
evals.expected_output: A ruling that formal blocking review is not required for an internal-only single-consumer alpha, derived explicitly from the exposure and lifecycle axes, with advisory feedback offered and the condition that would make review mandatory later.
expectations: Concludes that formal blocking review is not required for an internal-only surface with a single known consumer set
Names both axes that produce the conclusion: surface exposure (internal / partner / public) and lifecycle stage (alpha / beta / GA)
States that review is recommended but advisory at alpha, so an internal alpha gets advisory feedback rather than a blocking checklist
States that review becomes required at the beta gate if the surface ever becomes externally consumable
Attributes the audience-by-release-level keying to Google's AIP-100
Rejects the position that an internal API needs no contract, on the grounds that internal consumers are still consumers
Suggests tagging audience in the spec itself so the review trigger becomes mechanical, citing the x-api-audience convention
Notes that because the consumers are enumerable and deployed by the same team, defects can be fixed in place rather than routed through deprecation machinery
Declines to endorse the architecture lead's blocking gate as a compromise position
Keeps any findings it does raise in the Improvement bucket absent a cited rule
Assigns no numeric maturity score or readiness percentage to the internal API
Asks for the spec, reference docs, or sample requests and responses rather than reviewing from the endpoint name alone

evals.prompt:
Coastline Retail here, reviewing our public /v1 before we publish it. Pagination situation:

- GET /products uses ?page=3&per_page=50
- GET /orders uses ?cursor=eyJpZCI6...&limit=50
- GET /stores returns all 1,400 stores in one array, no params at all
- Ask /products for per_page=5000 and we quietly hand back 100
- GET /orders?statuss=shipped (note the typo) returns the full unfiltered list
- Every list response carries a `total` computed with a COUNT; orders is 240M rows and that is our slowest query by a wide margin
- /orders cursors are just base64'd row IDs, and ?sort=-created_at and ?sort=total_amount both happily accept the same cursor

Product insists on keeping offset on /products because the web admin has numbered pages and jump-to-page. What's the verdict?
evals.expected_output: A pagination and filtering review that flags the unbounded collection, the silent clamp, and the silently ignored filter as cited-rule findings, treats the retained offset as a recorded accepted deviation rather than an open failure, and requires the sort to be bound into the cursor.
expectations: Flags the unpaginated GET /stores as a Must-change against the rule that every collection endpoint is paginated
Flags the silent clamp of per_page=5000 down to 100 and requires a 400 response instead of a silently clamped value
Flags the silently ignored `statuss` typo and requires 400 or 422 for a filter on an unknown field
Explains that silently ignoring unknown filters makes a client typo indistinguishable from a genuinely empty result set
Flags the mixed offset-and-cursor pagination as a cross-surface consistency finding rather than praising it as client flexibility
Handles the retained offset pagination on /products as an accepted deviation with a recorded rationale, not as an unresolved failure or a blanket rejection
States that the recorded deviation becomes binding precedent for future admin-facing collections rather than a silent inconsistency
Flags that a cursor minted under one sort must not be replayable under a different sort, and requires the sort to be encoded into the cursor
Treats the `total` COUNT as a deliberate cost decision and proposes making it opt-in, for example via ?include_total=true
Requires a has_more flag or equivalent so clients never infer completion from a short page
Requires the response shape for empty results, last page, and out-of-range page requests to be specified rather than left undefined
States that filters are applied before the page is computed
Buckets every finding as Must-change or Improvement with a cited rule, and uses no numeric severity scale

evals.prompt:
Awkward situation at Quilsworth. A staff engineer left this on a teammate's API design PR and it has been stuck for 8 days:

"BLOCKING: snake_case is dated, switch the whole thing to camelCase. Also nest /refunds under /payments, reads better. And we settled the pagination question differently last year, so going back to cursors here."

The teammate's design is internally consistent snake_case throughout, /refunds is a top-level resource with a payment_id filter, and the pagination approach was explicitly signed off in a review 14 months ago. Two people have now escalated this to me. How do I unstick it, and how do I stop it happening again?
evals.expected_output: A ruling that an uncited block is not a valid block, downgrading each of the three objections, plus the standing mechanisms (deviation rationale convention, published escalation path and override authority) that prevent recurrence.
expectations: States that a blocking objection carrying no cited written rule or precedent is not a valid block
Downgrades the camelCase demand to an Improvement at most, because the only citable rule is consistency of the choice
Confirms the teammate's internally consistent snake_case already satisfies that consistency rule
Rejects the /refunds nesting demand as a block, noting the existing structure sits within the 2-3 level depth limit
Treats reopening the pagination decision as re-litigation of a settled prior review and declines it absent a significant, still-consequential mistake
States that the burden of justification falls on the party deviating from a cited rule, not on the designer defending against an uncited objection
Names the aip.dev/not-precedent rationale convention as the mechanism for recording an accepted deviation
Recommends publishing the escalation path and a named override authority so disagreements resolve in days
Identifies taste-based blocking comments as a named failure mode that recreates both rubber-stamping and bottlenecking
Gives the calibration line: firm on decisions affecting clients or security, forgiving on stylistic preference
Proposes no numeric score, rubric, or severity rating as the means of settling the dispute
Notes the 8-day stall against the under-a-week turnaround target for a small API

evals.prompt: Brightfold, developer platform team. We're about to run our first formal design review. In scope: our REST /v1 (28 endpoints, OpenAPI 3.1 checked into the repo), a new GraphQL gateway a squad has been building for 6 weeks, and our internal gRPC services that partners will eventually reach through a transcoding gateway. I want one consolidated review covering all three so we get consistency across the board. Where do we start?
evals.expected_output: A scoping step that confirms the paradigm, keeps only the REST surface in this review, hands the other two to the named sibling skills, runs the linter before human judgment, and asks for real production responses rather than trusting the spec.
expectations: Scopes the review to the REST surface only and declines to apply this checklist to the GraphQL and gRPC surfaces
Hands the GraphQL gateway to samber/developer-platform-skills@public-graphql-api-design
Hands the gRPC surface to samber/developer-platform-skills@public-grpc-api-design
Explains the handoff as a conventions mismatch that would make this checklist actively mislead, not as a convenience or a scope cut
Points at samber/developer-platform-skills@api-integration-surface-strategy for whether a surface belongs on the roadmap at all before it is reviewed
Runs a spec linter such as Spectral or Zally against the OpenAPI 3.1 file before any human-judgment check
States that linting owns the mechanical findings and human reviewers own the semantic ones, and does not invert that split
Cites the limitation that a linter cannot judge whether an operation makes sense to a consumer
Asks for 5-10 real production responses across endpoints rather than reviewing from the spec alone
Explains that a spec can claim a consistency the production traffic does not actually have
Inventories the endpoints and tags each as collection, mutating, or both
Asks its clarifying questions in one batch rather than one question per message

evals.prompt: Ardenway Labs. Public REST API, about 40 endpoints, documented in a Notion page a PM keeps updated by hand. No OpenAPI, no schema files, and honestly we'd rather write the spec after launch when things settle. Error bodies today: /v1/accounts throws {"error": "..."}, /v1/transfers returns {"errors": [{"code": 4012, "detail": "..."}]}, and a couple of endpoints return null with a 200 when the resource doesn't exist. We're ISO 27001 audited so we care a lot about not leaking internals. Give us the review.
evals.expected_output: A full checklist walk that logs the missing spec as a finding rather than refusing to proceed, treats mixed error envelopes as the top review-level error finding, stays at envelope-shape depth, and keeps the five sibling checks to one line each.
expectations: Logs the absence of a machine-readable spec as an Improvement finding in its own right
Proceeds with the checklist walk rather than refusing to review without a spec
Flags the three different error shapes as the top review-level error finding, citing the rule against mixing patterns
Explains that mixed error patterns leave the consumer unable to predict behavior across endpoints
Flags returning null with a 200 for a missing resource and requires 404 with the surface's standard envelope
Names RFC 9457 rather than RFC 7807 when referring to the problem-details envelope
States that RFC 9457 obsoletes RFC 7807
Keeps the error review at envelope-shape level and defers code taxonomy, message wording, and retry signaling to samber/developer-platform-skills@api-error-design
Does not design an error-code catalog, subcode scheme, or retryability flag as part of this review
Checks that no 500 body leaks a stack trace, database error text, internal path, or config, and labels that a security finding rather than only a developer-experience one
Covers all five sibling-boundary checks - versioning, idempotency, auth model, rate-limit signaling, documentation - at roughly one line each
Rejects writing the spec after launch with the point that the schema is the documentation and is written first
Walks all eight checklist dimensions rather than only the dimensions the prompt raised

evals.prompt: Pellworth. GA launch of our public API is Thursday, 6 days out, press embargo already set. Engineering finished the implementation 3 weeks ago and we only just got the design review back. It lists 9 items. Four cite our internal style guide: two casing inconsistencies, one verb-in-URI, and one endpoint returning 200 with an error body. The other five are the reviewer's own suggestions with no rule behind them, things like "consider adding a next link" and "I'd expose expand parameters". The VP of Eng wants to know whether we can ship Thursday with all 9 open and clean them up in the first maintenance release.
evals.expected_output: A ship-gate ruling that splits the 9 by whether a rule is cited, holds the four cited items to zero-open-at-GA while letting the five uncited ones ship, offers a documented deviation as the alternative to fixing before the date, and names the late-review failure mode.
expectations: Splits the 9 items into 4 Must-change and 5 Improvement strictly on whether a written rule is cited
States the ship gate as zero Must-change findings open at GA, with Improvement findings permitted to ship open
Allows the five uncited reviewer suggestions to ship open without a fix
Offers recording a documented deviation as a legitimate alternative to fixing a Must-change before the date
Names expediency - a deadline that cannot accommodate the better design - as one of the enumerated deviation reasons available
Requires any such deviation to carry a written rationale that leaves a trace, rather than a verbal or informal exception
Refuses to let the 200-with-error endpoint ship unresolved without either a fix or a recorded deviation
Identifies the review arriving three weeks after implementation was finished as a named failure mode of review programs
Attributes the late-review pattern to Google's documented pre-reform state, where teams were forced to start over
Prescribes triggering future reviews at design time against the spec, before the code exists
Assigns no numeric readiness score or percentage to the launch decision
Checks that the review walked every checklist dimension, treating a skipped dimension as an incomplete review rather than a lean one
